chunks: From him, from Muhammad ibn 'Isa, from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Hashim, from Salim Abi Khadijah, from Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

"When you are the Imam of a people, it is upon you to recite [the Quran] in the first two rak'ahs, and upon those behind you to say: 'Subhanallah, wal-hamdu lillah, wa la ilaha illallah, wallahu akbar' while they are standing. And when it is in the last two rak'ahs, it is upon those behind you to recite Fatihat al-Kitab, and upon the Imam to glorify [God] like the people glorify in the last two rak'ahs."

key_terms.إِمَامَ قَوْمٍ: Imam of a people (leader of congregational prayer)
key_terms.التَّسْبِيحُ: Glorification (referring to the recitation of the four phrases)
key_terms.فَاتِحَةَ الْكِتَابِ: The Opening of the Book (Surah Al-Fatiha)

ai.seo_question: What is the difference between the Imam's and the followers' recitation duties in the first and last two rak'ahs of prayer?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* details the specific liturgical division of labor in congregational prayer, reflecting the scholarly debate between the Ja'fari practice of silent Tasbihat al-Arba' by followers and the Sunni practice of loud Quranic recitation. It highlights the Imam's role in leading the congregation through both recitation and glorification, emphasizing the communal harmony of the prayer ritual. This specific arrangement underscores the distinct jurisprudential identity of the Shia school regarding the auditory experience of the congregant during the four rak'ahs.
